title: The Last Free Childhood
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart opens with students who spent an afternoon digging a hole on the playground with no adult direction and calls it their favorite day of the year. He argues that his generation of elder Millennials is the last to remember a pre-digital childhood of free play and has a responsibility to say what has been lost. Drawing on Peter Gray, Jonathan Haidt and Lenore Skenazy, he contends that kids are over-monitored and under-trusted, not because the world is more dangerous but because adults have forgotten how to trust one another. His school's Let Grow Play Club, with no screens and no adult agenda, is offered as a modest remedy with reported gains in cooperation and behavior. The piece ends as a call to loosen adult grip and let children fall, fail and figure things out.
points: The central claim is that childhood anxiety tracks the collapse of unsupervised play, so freedom is a need and not a luxury.
Stinehart reframes overprotection as a failure of community trust, since crime rates are low while fear keeps rising.
He compares adult-run organized play to processed food: technically food but lacking real nutritional value.
The school's Play Club is a concrete model of backing off, reporting fewer behavior issues and more cooperation without adding programming.
Memory of free childhood is treated as a responsibility to act while that living memory still exists.
quotes: Nobody taught them that. Nobody scheduled it. It happened because adults got out of the way.
Today’s children are monitored by design. Not because parents have changed for the worse, but because the culture around us has shifted so deeply that trusting kids now feels radical.

We have domesticated childhood, trimming away its wildness, its danger, its creative wastefulness. Most “play” children get today is organized, adult-led, and closely supervised…and we are paying the price.
And the irony is brutal: by trying to eliminate every risk, we have introduced a far bigger one, raising a generation who feel incapable of facing real life.
At the school where I teach, we started Play Club with a simple idea: What if we trusted kids again? No screens. No organized activities. No adult-driven agendas.

The overly-supervised, regulated, and often adult-led play we allow kids today is like processed food - technically it’s food, but it lacks most of the nutritional value and health benefits of real food. And if we’re not careful, we will become the generation who stood by while that trade became permanent.

Kids are anxious, disconnected, lonelier than ever, not resilient, not independent, and not because they have too much freedom, but because they have too little. And the saddest part? Again - the world outside has never been safer.
